So they injected a scaffold — a frame for cells to build on. It has a name, MAPS, for microporous annealed particle scaffolds, but the picture is simple: tiny gel beads that lock together into a sponge full of open channels. Cells can crawl in, hold on, and build.

Then they added signals borrowed from astrocytes. These are the star-shaped support cells of the brain. They react fast to injury and talk to their neighbours by releasing extracellular vesicles, or EVs — very small packages carrying proteins, fats and genetic material. The team grew astrocytes in the lab and collected their EVs. Instead of squirting them loose into the wound, they stuck the EVs onto the surface of the gel beads. The signals stayed put, exactly where arriving cells would meet them.

One pairing worked best. Two molecules, IL-4 and C1q, pulled immune cells deep into the injury. Macrophages came, as expected. So did neutrophils — and they stayed.

That was the surprise. Neutrophils are usually blamed for making stroke damage worse in the first hours. Here they arrived later, into a scaffold soaked in astrocyte signals, and appeared to help. To test it, the researchers cut down that neutrophil-rich group of immune cells. New blood vessel growth fell sharply, and the scaffold was reshaped much less. The cells were not bystanders.

In the treated mice, blood vessels grew right through the pocket. So did axons, the fibres brain cells use to send signals, both inside the injury and around it. Then the walking test: mice cross a grid, and the count is how often a forepaw slips through a gap. The treated mice kept improving. By eight weeks, statistics could not tell them apart from healthy mice. The gain held for the rest of the study.

One control matters most. EVs given without the scaffold did not repair blood vessels the same way. So the gel was not a delivery truck. The open structure and the signals held in place were doing the work together.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Mice, and mice only. No sample size is given here. The gel was injected straight into the damaged part of the brain — a far bigger step in a person. Safety is untested. Which immune cell contributes what is still unclear. And it has not been tried in larger animals, whose strokes look more like ours. Segura's lab is now working with EVs from astrocytes grown from human stem cells, a source that would scale better and give more control over what the packages carry.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The same cell can wreck a place or help rebuild it. What decides is when it arrives, and what it finds waiting.

recall.q: Neutrophils are known for making stroke damage worse. What in this study suggested they were helping to repair instead?
recall.a: When the researchers cut down the neutrophil-rich immune cells, new blood vessel growth dropped sharply and the scaffold was reshaped much less. The cells also arrived late, into a scaffold loaded with astrocyte signals — so timing and surroundings, not the cell type itself, seemed to decide whether they harmed or helped.

cards.title: A youth protein revived brain cleanup cells in mice
cards.body: The brain keeps its own cleaning crew: immune cells called microglia that swallow dead material and debris. Take away TIMP2 — a protein researchers link with youth — and those cells turn inflamed and stop clearing. Inject TIMP2 into old mice, and the clearing comes back.
cards.evidence: single study · mice · TIMP2 deleted, then injected into aged mice · no sample size reported

sections.text:
One picture from this study shows a single cell from an old mouse's brain, lit in two colours. Green marks its lysosomes — small sacs inside a cell that dissolve whatever the cell swallows. Purple marks what sits inside them: pieces of synapse, the tiny junctions where brain cells meet. The cell is digesting the brain's litter. That is exactly its job. This mouse had been given the protein this story is about.

Cells like it are called microglia. They are the brain's own immune cells and its housekeepers. They clear dead material, support the circuits neurons build, and arrive first at any injury. Old brains get worse at all of it. Tired microglia can slip into what the researchers call maladaptive states: instead of settling trouble, they keep the inflammation burning. Thinking suffers.

Age is the biggest risk factor for Alzheimer's and other diseases that kill brain cells. Why has stayed a hard puzzle. A team at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai went after one suspect: TIMP2, a protein they link with youth.

They tested it both ways. First they took it away. They bred mice without TIMP2 — some missing it only in their microglia, some only in their neurons. The second kind asks the sharper question: do microglia depend on TIMP2 that other cells make? The microglia changed fast. They cleared debris badly. Their gene activity carried the marks of senescence — the worn-out state where a cell stops doing its work and still does not die. The fluid between the cells filled with inflammatory and stress proteins. Remove one protein, and cells took on the signature of a brain that is old and hurt.

Then the other direction. They injected TIMP2 into aged mice, into the body rather than straight into the brain. The microglia moved back out of their inflamed state, and they swallowed and cleared waste better.

Joseph Castellano, the senior author, keeps the claim small: TIMP2 "may help restore aspects of microglial function" that age has damaged. The hedge is doing real work.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: Three ways of looking. Single-nuclei RNA sequencing reads which genes are switched on inside one cell nucleus at a time — that is how the senescence pattern showed up. In vivo microdialysis is a fine probe left in a living animal's brain that samples the fluid around the cells; that is how they caught inflammatory and stress proteins rising outside the cells, not only inside. Functional tests then asked the plain question: can these microglia still eat and clear?

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: All of this is mice, and the team's own line is that more studies are needed. What was measured is cell behaviour: clearing, inflammation, gene activity. The report does not say whether the treated old mice thought or remembered any better. A cell that cleans well is a good sign, not a cure.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Some of what we call an ageing brain may be a cleaning crew that quietly stopped cleaning.

recall.q: Deleting TIMP2 made microglia look aged. What did that alone not show, and what did the second experiment add?
recall.a: Deletion only shows the protein is needed; it cannot show the damage can be undone. The team then injected TIMP2 into aged mice, and the microglia moved out of their inflamed state and cleared waste better. Loss and restoration together make the case.

cards.title: Your mother still watches you for signs of improvement
cards.body: Florida Scott-Maxwell says a mother is not free to let her children be. She is under a law — the life that passed through her must come to something — and that one law makes both her love and her damage. It is why, however old she gets, she is still checking her middle-aged children for signs of improvement.

sections.text:
An old woman watches her middle-aged son across the room. What she is looking for is signs of improvement.

Florida Scott-Maxwell wrote that in The Measure of My Days. It is the account of her own life, published in 1968, close to the end of it. She had been a playwright, then a suffragist — one of the women who campaigned for the vote — then a psychologist. She is not describing bad mothers. She is describing all of them, herself included.

Her claim is that a mother is not free. She is under a painful law: the life that passed through her must come to something. She did not choose the law and she cannot quit it. Both her love and her damage come out of it.

Then comes the image that stops you softening any of this. A mother who cannot let her child go, who swallows the child whole, is like a frightened cat that eats its own young to keep them safe. The act is monstrous. The motive is protection. Scott-Maxwell is not excusing the harm. She is showing that it grows on the same stem as the love.

That brings the sentence at the heart of the passage: "It is not easy to give closeness and freedom, safety plus danger." Each pair names two things a child needs, and they pull in opposite directions. Maria Popova, who gathered the passage, hears in it the balance of closeness and independence that Kahlil Gibran said romantic love needs — because the way we love as adults echoes the way we were first held.

That is also why the watching never stops. However old she is, she checks her grown children for signs of improvement. She has to know that the seeds of value sown in her have been winnowed — winnowing is the farm work of throwing grain into the air so the wind takes the worthless husks and the good seed falls back. She needs proof that something real came through her, and she carries that hope to the end.

Here is the part Scott-Maxwell calls odd, very odd. A mother stays surprised, and even a little wronged, that her sons and daughters turned out to be ordinary people. Many mothers half expect the newborn to be a redeemer — someone who puts the world right.

She does not mock them for it. She wonders whether they are right: that the rare quality a mother once glimpsed in her child is still working somewhere inside the burdened adult. Maurice Sendak said something near it — that life is largely a matter of "having your child self intact and alive and something to be proud of."

That is the shift Popova is after. Your mother is not a saint and not a saviour. She is a person who loved you the best way she knew, with the cards she was dealt. Seeing that takes a whole life. Seeing it without bitterness is what a life can win.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: She never put the hope down. That is the burden, and it is also the love.

recall.q: Scott-Maxwell compares a mother who holds on too tight to a frightened cat that eats its own young. What is she saying with that image — and what is she not saying?
recall.a: That the harm and the love come from one source: she is under a law that the life that passed through her must come to something, and fear turns that into holding on too tight. She is explaining the act, not excusing it — the image is meant to be monstrous.

cards.title: Beauvoir at 19: friendship, not love, got it right
cards.body: At nineteen, in her student journal, Simone de Beauvoir asked what love really is. Her answer: not much. Real connection, she decided, is two free people who keep freeing each other. The romantic ideal fails that test, because it asks one self to dissolve into the other. She found the real thing not in a lover but in her best friend, Zaza.

sections.text:
A packed recital hall in Paris, early last century. In the front rows sit girls in their best dresses, curled and ribboned, waiting their turn at the piano. Behind them, teachers in stiff black silk and white gloves. A girl in a blue taffeta dress plays a piece her mother had called too hard for her. She plays it perfectly, for once. Then she turns and sticks her tongue out at her mother.

The curls in the front row trembled. The teachers' faces froze. The girl was Zaza. Watching her was Simone de Beauvoir, who remembered the moment for the rest of her life.

Beauvoir was nineteen when she started writing about love in her journal, published later as Diary of a Philosophy Student. She had an intellectual crush on a young man who would become a famous philosopher himself. She was also suspicious of the whole business. To say that I love him — what does that mean? Does the word have a meaning at all?

Her doubt ran like this. Suppose you love people for what is deepest in them — not their intelligence, just the plain fact that they exist. Then you must love them all equally, since existing is already complete. So the strange thing is not that we love everyone. It is that we prefer one.

Asked what love is, she answered: not much. Sensitivity, imagination, tiredness, the effort to depend on somebody. A taste for the other person's mystery, and the need to admire.

What she wanted instead came from Hegel, the German philosopher. For a mind to be free, he held, it must free the other mind too. Freedom is not held alone. It is something two people do for each other. From that, Beauvoir drew her formula for the ideal bond: absolute reciprocity — two minds recognising each other as the same kind of thing, equal in both directions.

The romantic ideal we inherited swaps that for something else: swallowing. One self dissolves into the other, and the loss gets called depth. Beauvoir, at nineteen, refused the trade. Love should not make everything else disappear, she wrote, only tint it with new shades. She wanted "a love that accompanies me through life, not that absorbs all my life."

She found it, and not with a lover. She found it with the girl in the blue dress. She only understood it during one of the separations their families and school terms kept forcing on them. She had never even thought to tell herself that she missed Zaza. "I needed her presence to realize how much I needed her," she wrote.

The neat ranking she grew up inside — friendship respectable, romance splendid, family love sacred — fell apart. Friendship, she decided, gets right what love keeps getting wrong: it asks everything of you and demands nothing. No jealousy, no conditions, no testing. She did not need Zaza to feel anything definite back, and admiring her never made her smaller in her own eyes.

Zaza died suddenly at twenty-one, halfway through Beauvoir's second year of philosophy. The woman who spent the rest of her life breaking rules first learned it could be done from a girl who stuck her tongue out at a piano recital.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The ideal she refused has a defence. The self-loss she calls swallowing is exactly what its admirers prize — the proof that this love is unlike every other. And she was nineteen, writing about a crush, not about a life shared across decades. She went on to build her own rule-breaking union of minds. So her real target may have been the demand that one side give way, not romance itself.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The test is not how much of you a bond takes. It is how much of you it leaves standing.

recall.q: Beauvoir wanted a love that goes alongside her life instead of swallowing it. What was she rejecting, and where did she find her alternative?
recall.a: She rejected the romantic ideal in which one self dissolves into the other. Her alternative, taken from Hegel, was two free people who keep freeing each other — absolute reciprocity. She found it not in romance but in her friendship with Zaza, which asked everything of her and demanded nothing back.

cards.title: Deposits from Indians abroad are testing the RBI
cards.body: Indians living abroad are moving foreign currency into Indian bank accounts. All that money lands as spare cash in the banking system, and the Reserve Bank now has to decide what to do with it. One auction will show how big the pile really is.

sections.text:
Indians living abroad are pouring money into FCNR(B) accounts — foreign currency deposits that non-residents hold at Indian banks. That money lands as spare cash inside the banking system. Keeping that spare cash — liquidity — in a comfortable range is the Reserve Bank of India's job.

The test is a variable rate reverse repo auction. The RBI invites banks to park their spare cash with it for a fixed period, and banks bid on the rate. How much they offer, and how cheaply, tells the RBI how big the surplus really is. That reading may shape how it manages liquidity from here.

Two heavier tools are held back: dollar swaps with banks, and sales of government bonds.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Good news with an awkward side. The inflow is welcome, but the RBI still has to decide how much of that cash to leave in the system — and one auction sets the tone for the months ahead.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: How much cash banks actually park in the auction, and whether the RBI stops there or reaches for dollar swaps and bond sales.

recall.q: Deposits from Indians abroad sound like plain good news. Why do they become a problem the RBI has to manage?
recall.a: The money lands as spare cash inside the banking system, and holding that spare cash in a comfortable range is the RBI's job. The reverse repo auction is how it measures the surplus.
